result:
I've put the final answer in `final.py`. It scores **0.5799 on the search split, up from 0.365 for LRU**, using **18 of the 24 scorer calls**. I spent about 9 minutes of the 15-minute default and stopped early because the last three rounds of changes didn't improve anything.

| | search score |
|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 |
| First champion (W-TinyLFU) | 0.5034 |
| First version that adjusted itself (W-TinyLFU, self-tuning window) | 0.5239 |
| Plain LIRS | 0.5666 |
| LIRS tuned by shadow copies | 0.5790–0.5793 |
| **Final: follows whichever shadow policy is doing best** | **0.5799** |

There's no held-out split from the scorer, so I couldn't check the final pick on unseen traces. My own local test traces stand in for that: on traces I never tuned on, the final scores 0.482 against 0.473 for the next-best version. Those local traces track the real ones only loosely (they ranked LRU above W-TinyLFU at first), so treat that check as weak.

The final pick ties a slightly simpler version (0.5800). I kept the one with more shadow policies because it did better on my local held-out traces.

**Why it beats LRU:** for every request, `final.py` also runs a set of "shadow" caches. These track only which keys they would hold, not real cache contents. There are ten LIRS copies with different settings, plus W-TinyLFU, S3-FIFO, ARC and LRU. Each counts its own hits, with older hits fading out. The real cache copies whichever shadow is currently ahead: on a miss it throws out the key that shadow threw out. It only switches to a new leader when that one is clearly ahead, so it doesn't flip back and forth.
- **Loops and one-off scans:** LIRS keeps a fixed set of keys in the cache through repeated passes over data that doesn't fit. LRU loses all of it, which is why the shifting-loops trace scores 0.83.
- **Recency trace:** the real cache moves to settings that favour recently used keys, scoring 0.845. Plain LIRS got 0.77.
- **Hot keys mixed with scans:** it switches to W-TinyLFU when that is ahead.

Every shadow sees the same requests, so a sudden shift in what is popular doesn't mislead the choice. My earlier version tuned itself from its own hit rate and got this wrong (0.554), because the hit rate changes when the workload changes. On a 999-capacity, 80,000-request stress test the final ran in 0.7 s locally, well inside the 8-second limit.

**Approaches tried** (search scores, plus local harness scores for ones I didn't send to the scorer):
1. ARC: 0.446 locally; it went in as a shadow.
2. LIRS: 0.5666. This was the turning point.
3. S3-FIFO: 0.479. Best on recency, weak on loops; it went in as a shadow.
4. 2Q: not built.
5. W-TinyLFU with a self-tuning window: 0.524.
6. LFU with aging: not built.
7. CLOCK-Pro: not built.
8. LeCaR-style mix of policies: built in the form of the follow-the-leader cache, 0.580.
9. Dropped: LIRS tuned from its own hit rate (0.554–0.564), more extra shadows, and other leader-check intervals and fade rates.

Everything is in the working folder; `log.md` has one line per candidate with local and scorer scores.
